docs.t: Judge John D. Early (C.D. Cal.) — Protective orders and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge John D. Early, C.D. Cal.. Protective orders and proposed orders: Stipulated protective orders must meet Rule 26; the court will not enter one restricting public access to court records contrary to L.R. 79-5, and a discovery protective order should not try to control the handling of materials at trial. A model order is posted. Lodge proposed orders under CM/ECF procedures and email a Word version to JDE_Chambers@cacd.uscourts.gov. Word versions of proposed orders in criminal duty matters go to JDE_CrimDuty@cacd.uscourts.gov.

docs.t: Judge John D. Early (C.D. Cal.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge John D. Early, C.D. Cal.. Settlement conferences: When a conference has been ordered, the parties jointly contact the deputy with at least three proposed dates at least four weeks before the requested conference; an order follows once a date is accepted.

docs.t: Judge John D. Early (C.D. Cal.) — Contact and interpreters
docs.x: Judge John D. Early, C.D. Cal.. Contact and interpreters: Courtroom deputy: Amber Rodriguez (JDE_Chambers@cacd.uscourts.gov). Civil parties are responsible for securing interpreters.

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Hearings and tentative rulings
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Hearings and tentative rulings: Civil motions Tuesdays at 10:00 a.m. in Santa Ana unless directed otherwise; no need to clear a date, but check closed dates. The court may continue motions or decide them on the papers. Tentative rulings, if issued, are posted at the page’s “Tentative Rulings” link and/or about half an hour before the hearing in the courtroom. If all parties submit, tell the deputy and no appearance is needed. Telephone appearance requests must be filed at least two business days before the hearing. Special appearances are typically not permitted. Equipment requests go to the deputy at least three business days ahead.

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Chambers copies and briefs
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Chambers copies and briefs: All parties are excused from delivering chambers copies of e-filed documents until further order. Email Word versions of proposed orders to KES_Chambers@cacd.uscourts.gov. The page restates L.R. 11-6.1: typed memoranda, including motions, oppositions, replies, and trial briefs, may not exceed 7,000 words, with an L.R. 11-6.2 certificate (25 pages for handwritten or typewritten briefs). Extensions only rarely; limits apply to self-represented parties. Joint discovery stipulations are governed by L.R. 37-2.1 instead.

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Discovery: meet and confer and format (trap)
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Discovery: meet and confer and format (trap): Caption discovery filings and proposed protective orders “[Discovery Document: Referred to Magistrate Judge Karen E. Scott].” Unanswered letters or emails do not satisfy the meet-and-confer duty; follow up with a phone call. The L.R. 37-1 in-person requirement for same-county counsel is suspended, and failure to meet in person is no ground to grant or deny a motion, but parties may not agree to confer solely by email, letter, or voicemail; a same-time phone, Zoom, or in-person discussion is required. In joint stipulations, group requests that raise the same issue and argue each point once rather than cutting and pasting; include definitions of any defined terms. Check whether the district judge’s cut-off is the last day to file or to hear discovery motions. Under the IDC procedure, a motion is deemed filed whe

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Informal discovery conference (IDC)
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Informal discovery conference (IDC): By agreement, after the L.R. 37-1 conference, the movant emails the deputy with at least three proposed dates and times (9:30 a.m. preferred). Once confirmed, the movant e-files a “Notice of Discovery Motion and Telephonic Conference” (Discovery Motions event) identifying the requests and legal dispute. At least 24 hours before, the parties e-file letter briefs of no more than 3 pages (excluding title page and exhibits), linked to the Notice as supplemental briefs. Arguments must have been discussed by phone or in person first. The court may rule or order further briefing. If the opponent has served no objections or responses and has ignored emails and at least one phone call, the movant may use the IDC without consent.

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Discovery orders and sanctions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Discovery orders and sanctions (trap): Proposed orders on discovery motions must state the specific relief for each request (for example, supplemental responses, production, and a privilege log by a date), not just “motion granted.” Sanctions requests must cite authority and explain how the standard is met. To recover expenses, include supporting evidence of the amount in the joint stipulation or letter brief, or state the amount and offer evidence later.

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Ex parte applications
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Ex parte applications: Comply with L.R. 7-19 and 7-19.1; usually decided on the papers. Oppositions are due within 24 hours of electronic filing, extended to the same time on the next day that is not a weekend or holiday. Discovery disputes generally should not come by ex parte application.

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Protective orders and sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Protective orders and sealing (trap): Protective orders must describe protected material with particularity (for example, “personnel records”), not just “confidential or proprietary information,” and include a separate “GOOD CAUSE STATEMENT.” The court cannot agree to seal all confidential documents. If you use the posted LACBA standard form, identify any changes by description or redline. Unredacted versions must highlight the proposed redactions, or the sealing application may be denied without prejudice. Proposed orders on discovery-related sealing applications must use a chart listing each item (with page/line cites), its docket location, a description with Bates numbers, and a grant/deny space for each; good-cause declarations under L.R. 79-5.2.2 should follow the same item-by-item structure. Provide the native file to the other side on request.

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Continuances, settlement, and contact
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Continuances, settlement, and contact: Continuances: stipulation and proposed order at least three business days before the hearing. Calendar conflicts: email the deputy immediately and seek a stipulation; otherwise apply ex parte. Settlement conferences: email the deputy proposed dates at least three weeks ahead; the order may set brief deadlines and a counsel-only pre-conference call. Do not call chambers or the law clerks unless directed.

docs.t: Judge Karen E. Scott (C.D. Cal.) — Social Security, summary judgment, and AI
docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. Social Security, summary judgment, and AI: Social Security (filed on or after December 1, 2022): plaintiff’s brief must have an “Issues Presented” section listing each claimed ALJ error and must state the relief sought; unlisted or unsupported issues may be deemed waived, and new issues may not be raised in reply. Comply with L.R. 11-6 (word-count certificate) and confer with the Commissioner’s counsel at least seven days before filing. Summary judgment: follow L.R. 56-1 et seq. (June 2023); on request, exchange native Word versions of the statements of uncontroverted facts and genuine disputes. Anyone signing a filing drafted in whole or part with AI certifies under Rule 11 that the cited authorities were checked and verified.

docs.x: Judge Karen E. Scott, C.D. Cal.. docs.t: Judge Margo A. Rocconi (C.D. Cal.) — Discovery Standing Order (trap)
docs.x: Judge Margo A. Rocconi, C.D. Cal.. Discovery Standing Order (trap): Read the Standing Order before filing any discovery motion; noncompliance can bring fee-shifting sanctions. Emails supplement but do not replace phone or in-person conferences; perfunctory email exchanges are inadequate. Boilerplate objections and conclusory proportionality, burden, cost, or overbreadth objections will be summarily rejected or deemed waived. Pro forma Rule 26(f) plans are not allowed; issues first raised in a motion to compel that could have been raised in the plan may be deemed waived. Ex parte applications to shorten time on a motion to compel because of the cut-off will be summarily rejected absent diligence and good cause. Lack of an FRE 502(d) order or 502(e) agreeme

docs.x: Judge Patricia Donahue, C.D. Cal.. Consent cases: deadlines and ADR (trap): Discovery cut-offs are completion dates, including hearings on related motions; depositions and written discovery must start early enough to allow motions before the cut-off. Expert disclosures must be in writing; trial dates will not move because expert discovery is incomplete. All motions, including summary judgment and Daubert, must be heard by the motion cut-off. docs.t: Judge Patricia Donahue (C.D. Cal.) — Pretrial filings (consent cases)
docs.x: Judge Patricia Donahue, C.D. Cal.. Pretrial filings (consent cases): Motions in limine: four per side absent leave, each non-compound; motions and oppositions 2,800 words, replies 2,100 words. Usually decided at the FPTC. Due 5 court days before the FPTC: proposed pretrial conference order, one-page joint statement of the case, joint witness list (order’s format, time estimates, testimony descriptions), glossary, joint exhibit list, and optional voir dire. Under the trial order, jury instructions and verdict forms are due 5 days before the FPTC (plaintiff serves them 14 days before the L.R. 16-2 meeting; defendant objects within 7 days). The November 2025 schedule form instead sets an Initial Pretrial Conference, with motions in limine, contentions of fact and law, jury instructions, and verdict forms due 14 calendar days before it and oppositions 7 days before; follow the schedule set i

docs.t: Judge Patricia Donahue (C.D. Cal.) — Jury instructions and exhibits
docs.x: Judge Patricia Donahue, C.D. Cal.. Jury instructions and exhibits: Use Ninth Circuit models, then CACI or BAJI; each instruction on a separate numbered page with its source, plus an index; file agreed, then each side’s disputed instructions with short supporting and opposing statements; email Word versions. The court gives its own introductory instructions. Exhibits tagged lower right and internally paginated; for paper exhibits, two binder sets for the court and one for the opponent. An exhibit conference with trial counsel is held at 1:30 p.m. on the Monday of the week before trial unless ordered otherwise.

docs.t: Judge Patricia Donahue (C.D. Cal.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Patricia Donahue, C.D. Cal.. Trial: Jury trial days generally Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., with three 15-minute breaks; on the first day counsel go on the record at 8:30 a.m. and selection starts at 9:00 a.m. Later, matters outside the jury’s presence are handled 8:00 to 8:30 a.m. Sidebars are discouraged. Usually eight jurors and three peremptories per side by Arizona blind strike; the court conducts voir dire, with up to 15 minutes of follow-up per side. Use the lectern; state objections and grounds only. Lodge depositions with the deputy on the first day of trial. A party without a next witness may be deemed to have rested.

Day one runs 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; later days 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with two 15-minute breaks and a 1-hour lunch. Lodge signed depositions on the first day of trial. Each evening, announce the next day’s witnesses and time estimates.

docs.t: Alaska — Losing costs you fees: Civil Rule 82
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Losing costs you fees: Civil Rule 82: Alaska shifts partial fees to the prevailing party in nearly every civil case. On a money judgment after a contested trial, the award is 20% of the first $25,000 and 10% of the rest. Without a money judgment, it is 30% (tried) or 20% (not tried) of reasonable actual fees. Budget for it, tell the client in the fee agreement (RPC 1.5(b)), and file your own motion within 10 days after the clerk’s distribution date on the judgment or the fees are waived. (Alaska R. Civ. P. 82(b), (c); Alaska R. Prof. Conduct 1.5(b))

docs.t: Alaska — Ignoring a Rule 68 offer can cost up to 75% of actual fees
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Ignoring a Rule 68 offer can cost up to 75% of actual fees: If the final judgment is at least 5% worse for you than an offer you rejected (10% with multiple defendants), you pay all costs plus 75%, 50%, or 30% of the offeror’s reasonable actual fees from the offer date. The percentage depends on whether the offer was served within 60 days after the initial-disclosure date in the pretrial order, more than 90 days before trial, or later. This applies to plaintiffs and defendants alike. (Alaska R. Civ. P. 68(b))

docs.t: Alaska — Five days to bump the judge
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Five days to bump the judge: The peremptory change of judge must be filed within 5 days after notice of assignment (or of your appearance, if you enter late), and before trial. Taking part in an evidentiary merits proceeding or a pretrial conference before the judge waives it. (Alaska R. Civ. P. 42(c)(3), (4))

docs.t: Alaska — Answer in 20 days, not 21
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Answer in 20 days, not 21: The answer is due 20 days after service (40 for the State, its officers and agencies, and some others). After a Rule 12 motion is denied, the answer is due 10 days after notice of the ruling. (Alaska R. Civ. P. 12(a))

docs.t: Alaska — Clocks run from the clerk’s certificate of distribution
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Clocks run from the clerk’s certificate of distribution: Time to appeal and to seek reconsideration or review runs from the “date of notice.” For written orders, that is the date in the clerk’s certificate of distribution, not the date the judge signed. But a motion to alter or amend under Rule 59(f) must be served within 10 days after entry, and a new-trial motion within 10 days after the distribution date. Reconsideration under Rule 77(k) is due within 10 days, is limited to 5 pages, and is deemed denied after 30 days. (Alaska R. Civ. P. 58.1(c), 59(b), (f), 77(k))

docs.t: Alaska — A notice of appeal needs a package, and fee proceedings don’t toll
docs.x: Alaska land mine. A notice of appeal needs a package, and fee proceedings don’t toll: File in the Supreme Court within 30 days from the distribution date on the judgment. Include a docketing statement, the judgment, a statement of points on appeal, the fee or a waiver motion, a $750 cost bond (or supersedeas or deposit), a transcript designation, and proof of service. The clerk will refuse a notice that lacks these items. The appeal clock is not stopped while costs, prejudgment interest, or Rule 82 fees are being decided. Amend your points later to add the fee award. (Alaska R. App. P. 204(a)(1), (a)(5), (b), (c)(1), (e))

docs.t: Alaska — Ten days to seek interlocutory review
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Ten days to seek interlocutory review: A petition for review of a non-appealable order is due 10 days after the date of notice of the order, with a 15-page limit. A timely reconsideration motion in the trial court restarts the period. (Alaska R. App. P. 402, 403(a)(1))

docs.t: Alaska — Pro hac vice fee recurs every year
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Pro hac vice fee recurs every year: The Civil Rule 81 fee is the full annual active-member dues, charged per case per year until you tell the Bar the case is closed or you have withdrawn. Local counsel must co-sign every filing. (Alaska Bar Bylaws art. III, § 4; Alaska R. Civ. P. 81(a)(2))

docs.t: Alaska — Disclose thin malpractice coverage in writing
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Disclose thin malpractice coverage in writing: If you appear in Alaska without malpractice coverage of at least $100,000 per claim and $300,000 aggregate, you must tell the client in writing. The disclosure belongs in any written fee agreement over $1,000. (Alaska R. Prof. Conduct 1.4(c), 1.5(b))

docs.t: Alaska — Nonresident plaintiffs can be made to post security
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Nonresident plaintiffs can be made to post security: When the plaintiff lives out of state or is a foreign corporation, a defendant who demands it within 30 days after discovering the nonresidence stays the case until an undertaking of at least $200 is filed. The undertaking secures the costs and attorney fees that may be awarded against the plaintiff. (AS 09.60.060)

docs.t: Alaska — Wrong court for smaller cases
docs.x: Alaska land mine. Wrong court for smaller cases: Claims within the district court’s concurrent civil jurisdiction (up to $100,000 per defendant) may not be filed in superior court except as supreme court rules provide. Protective-order petitions are an exception. Check the rules before filing a smaller case in superior court. (AS 22.10.020(a); AS 22.15.030(a)(1))

docs.t: Alaska — E-filing mechanics
docs.x: Alaska land mine. E-filing mechanics: TrueFiling is mandatory for lawyers. Combine the motion, memorandum, and exhibits into one PDF, with the proposed order as a separate document in the same bundle. Files must be under 10 MB, and the cutoff is 11:59 p.m. Alaska Time. (Admin. Bull. No. 92 ¶¶ 1(a), 7(a), 13(a)–(b), 15)

docs.t: Alaska anti-SLAPP — No anti-SLAPP statute found in the Alaska Statutes
docs.x: Alaska anti-SLAPP. No anti-SLAPP statute found in the Alaska Statutes: Alaska has no special motion to strike, discovery stay, or speech-specific fee shifting in the statute chapters where such laws normally sit. AS 09.65 (Actions, Immunities, Defenses, and Duties) lists dozens of immunities, from emergency aid to defensive force, but none for speech or petitioning. AS 09.60 (Costs and Attorney Fees) has no SLAPP provision either, and no Title 9 chapter is devoted to the subject. Defend speech suits with ordinary Rule 12(b)(6) and Rule 56 motions. Civil Rule 82 fee shifting (and Rule 68 offers) still give the prevailing defendant partial fees, and AS 09.60.010(c) protects non-frivolous constitutional claimants (see the speech notes). docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (civil, to Supreme Court)
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (civil, to Supreme Court): 30 days from Date shown in the clerk’s certificate of distribution on the judgment (Alaska R. App. P. 204(a)(1)). File with the Clerk of the Appellate Courts with the full Rule 204(b) package and the $750 cost bond.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Cross-appeal / subsequent appeal
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Cross-appeal / subsequent appeal: 14 days from Filing of another party’s timely notice of appeal (or 30 days from distribution, whichever is later) (Alaska R. App. P. 204(a)(2)). Also the route to appeal a later costs or fees order.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Appeal to superior court from district court
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Appeal to superior court from district court: 30 days from Date in the clerk’s certificate of distribution on the judgment (Alaska R. App. P. 602(a)(1)).

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Appeal to superior court from an agency
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Appeal to superior court from an agency: 30 days from Mailing or distribution of the final decision (or of the reconsideration ruling or deemed denial) (Alaska R. App. P. 602(a)(2)). The clock starts only if the decision states it is final and that there are 30 days to appeal.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Motion for new trial
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Motion for new trial: 10 days from Date in the clerk’s certificate of distribution on the judgment (Alaska R. Civ. P. 59(b)). Served, not just filed. Tolls appeal time under App. R. 204(a)(3).

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Motion to alter or amend judgment
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Motion to alter or amend judgment: 10 days from Entry of judgment (Alaska R. Civ. P. 59(f)). Measured from entry, not from the distribution date.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Trial-court reconsideration
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Trial-court reconsideration: 10 days from Date of notice of the ruling (Alaska R. Civ. P. 77(k)). 5-page limit; deemed denied after 30 days; tolls appeal time.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Rule 82 attorney’s fee motion
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Rule 82 attorney’s fee motion: 10 days from Date in the clerk’s certificate of distribution on the judgment (Alaska R. Civ. P. 82(c)). Waived if late unless the court allows more time. Does not toll appeal time.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Cost bill in trial court
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Cost bill in trial court: 10 days from Date in the clerk’s certificate of distribution on the judgment (Alaska R. Civ. P. 79). Objections due 7 days after service.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Appellant’s opening brief
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Appellant’s opening brief: 30 days from Clerk’s notice of the brief due date (Alaska R. App. P. 212(a)(1)(A)). 50 numbered pages.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief: 30 days from Service of appellant’s brief (Alaska R. App. P. 212(a)(1)(A)). 50 numbered pages.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Reply brief (or notice of no reply)
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Reply brief (or notice of no reply): 20 days from Service of appellee’s brief (Alaska R. App. P. 212(a)(1)(A)). 20 pages.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Request for oral argument
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Request for oral argument: 10 days from Due date of the reply brief (or of the appellee’s brief if no reply is allowed) (Alaska R. App. P. 505(a)(2)). No argument without a timely request.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Petition for rehearing
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Petition for rehearing: 10 days from Date of notice of the opinion or decision (Alaska R. App. P. 506(b)). 5-page limit.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Petition for hearing
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Petition for hearing: 30 days from Date of notice of the intermediate appellate decision (or of the rehearing ruling) (Alaska R. App. P. 303(a)). 15 pages; response 30 days after service; extend up to 15 days by notice.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Petition for review (non-final order)
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Petition for review (non-final order): 10 days from Date of notice of the order (Alaska R. App. P. 403(a)(1)(A)). 15 pages; response and cross-petition 10 days after service.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Appellate cost bill / fee motion
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Appellate cost bill / fee motion: 10 days from Date of notice of the opinion or Rule 214 order (Alaska R. App. P. 508(f)(1)–(2)). Objections to the cost bill are due within 7 days.

docs.t: Alaska appeal deadline — Opposition to appellate motion
docs.x: Alaska appellate deadline. Opposition to appellate motion: 7 days from Service of the motion (Alaska R. App. P. 503(d)).

docs.t: Alabama — The 90-day deemed denial restarts your appeal clock without warning
docs.x: Alabama land mine. The 90-day deemed denial restarts your appeal clock without warning: A Rule 50, 52, 55, or 59 motion not ruled on within 90 days is denied by operation of law, and the 42-day appeal period runs from that date, even if the judge later holds a hearing or rules. Only express consent of all parties on the record, or an appellate-court extension, stops it. (Ala. R. Civ. P. 59.1; Ala. R. App. P. 4(a)(3))

docs.t: Alabama — 42 days to appeal, 14 for injunctions; no appellate extension
docs.x: Alabama land mine. 42 days to appeal, 14 for injunctions; no appellate extension: The notice of appeal is due 42 days after entry (not 30), but only 14 days for interlocutory injunction, receivership, and similar orders. A late notice must be dismissed, and appellate courts cannot extend the time; the trial court may add up to 30 days only for failure to learn of the entry. (Ala. R. App. P. 4(a)(1), 2(a)(1), 2(b), 26(b); Ala. R. Civ. P. 77(d))

docs.t: Alabama — Two different weekend rules for computing time
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Two different weekend rules for computing time: Under the civil rules, intermediate weekends and holidays are excluded for periods under 11 days; under the appellate rules, only for periods under 7 days. Three days are added after service by mail or through the e-filing system in the trial court. (Ala. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(2), 6(d); Ala. R. App. P. 26(a))

docs.t: Alabama — Plaintiff’s claims against a third-party defendant are compulsory
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Plaintiff’s claims against a third-party defendant are compulsory: If a defendant impleads a third party, the plaintiff’s failure to assert claims against that third-party defendant arising from the same transaction has the same effect as failing to plead a compulsory counterclaim. (Ala. R. Civ. P. 14(a)(3))

docs.t: Alabama — Two suits for the same cause: the first one bars the second
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Two suits for the same cause: the first one bars the second: A plaintiff may not prosecute two actions in Alabama courts at the same time for the same cause against the same party; the pendency of the earlier action is a defense to the later one, and simultaneous actions force an election. (Ala. Code § 6-5-440)

docs.t: Alabama — Local counsel must physically attend every hearing
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Local counsel must physically attend every hearing: Pro hac vice local counsel is not a name on the pleadings: local counsel must personally appear at all pretrial conferences, hearings, and trials unless excused, and shares joint and several responsibility. Filings made before you comply with Rule VII are stricken, and the Bar’s statement on your prior applications must be filed before the court can grant admission. (Rules Governing Admission, Rule VII.C, VII.D, VII.K)

docs.t: Alabama — Jury demand within 30 days of the last pleading
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Jury demand within 30 days of the last pleading: Serve a written jury demand no later than 30 days after service of the last pleading directed to the issue (10 days in an appeal to circuit court), and file it. Failure to demand, or failing to appear at trial, waives the jury. (Ala. R. Civ. P. 38(b), (d))

docs.t: Alabama — Supersedeas bond is 125% to 150% of the judgment
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Supersedeas bond is 125% to 150% of the judgment: To stay a money judgment pending appeal, the bond must be 150% of a judgment of $10,000 or less, or 125% of a larger one, approved by the trial-court clerk. The automatic stay lasts only 30 days after entry. (Ala. R. App. P. 8(a)(1); Ala. R. Civ. P. 62(a))

docs.t: Alabama — Want the Supreme Court to see your facts? Put them in the rehearing application
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Want the Supreme Court to see your facts? Put them in the rehearing application: If the Court of Civil Appeals misstated the facts or affirmed without opinion, your additional or corrected facts must be presented in the application for rehearing in that court and copied verbatim into the certiorari petition. Certiorari is due 14 days after the decision (or the rehearing ruling) and cannot be extended. (Ala. R. App. P. 39(c), 39(d)(5), 40(e))

docs.t: Alabama — Interlocutory permissive appeal only in Supreme Court cases
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Interlocutory permissive appeal only in Supreme Court cases: A Rule 5 permissive appeal is available only in civil cases within the Supreme Court’s original appellate jurisdiction, needs a trial-judge certification (presumptively within 28 days) stating the controlling question, and the petition is due 14 days after certification. Cases within the Court of Civil Appeals’ jurisdiction (e.g., $50,000 or less, domestic relations) cannot use it. (Ala. R. App. P. 5(a))

docs.t: Alabama — Wrongful death: 2 years and county limits
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Wrongful death: 2 years and county limits: Alabama wrongful-death actions belong to the personal representative, must be filed within 2 years after death, and only in a county where the decedent could have sued under the venue statutes (§§ 6-3-2, 6-3-7). (Ala. Code § 6-5-410(a), (d), (e))

docs.t: Alabama — Confidentiality exceptions are narrower than you are used to
docs.x: Alabama land mine. Confidentiality exceptions are narrower than you are used to: Alabama Rule 1.6 permits disclosure only to prevent a client crime likely to cause imminent death or substantial bodily harm and for the lawyer’s own claims and defenses; there is no financial-fraud, ethics-advice, or court-order exception in the rule text. (Ala. R. Prof. Cond. 1.6(b))

docs.t: Alabama anti-SLAPP — No anti-SLAPP statute found in the Code of Alabama
docs.x: Alabama anti-SLAPP. No anti-SLAPP statute found in the Code of Alabama: A search of the official Code of Alabama on the Legislature’s ALISON site (Nov. 10, 2026) for “SLAPP,” “strategic lawsuit,” “public expression,” “public participation,” and “special motion” found no special motion to dismiss or strike, discovery stay, or fee-shifting procedure for claims based on speech or petitioning. A full-text search of bills in all sessions on ALISON (“SLAPP,” “strategic lawsuits,” “public expression,” “matter of public concern,” “right of free speech”) surfaced no anti-SLAPP bill among the top results; that search ranks by relevance and only the first results were reviewed, so an introduced bill using other wording could have been missed. Defendants rely on ordinary Rule 12(b)(6) and Rule 56 motions. (Code of Alabama 1975 (ALISON search, Nov. 10, 2026); Ala. R. Civ. P. 12, 56)

docs.t: Alabama anti-SLAPP — Related protection that does exist: libel retraction demand
docs.x: Alabama anti-SLAPP. Related protection that does exist: libel retraction demand: Punitive damages for libel require proof that the defendant published with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard, and that the plaintiff made a written demand for a public retraction at least 5 days before suit and the defendant failed to publish a full and fair retraction within 5 days. This limits damages; it is not an early-dismissal procedure. (Ala. Code § 6-5-186)

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Notice of appeal from final civil judgment
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Notice of appeal from final civil judgment: 42 days from Entry of judgment (input into SJIS or e-transmission by judge) (Ala. R. App. P. 4(a)(1); Ala. R. Civ. P. 58(c)). Jurisdictional; no appellate extension (Rules 2(b), 26(b)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Notice of appeal after post-judgment motion
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Notice of appeal after post-judgment motion: 42 days from Entry of order disposing of last Rule 50/52/55/59 motion, or deemed-denial date (Ala. R. App. P. 4(a)(3); Ala. R. Civ. P. 59.1). Rule 60(b) motions do not toll.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Post-judgment motion deemed denied
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Post-judgment motion deemed denied: 90 days from Filing of the Rule 50/52/55/59 motion (Ala. R. Civ. P. 59.1). Unless all parties consent on the record or the appellate court extends. District court: 14 days.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Motion for new trial / to alter, amend, or vacate / renewed JML / amend findings
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Motion for new trial / to alter, amend, or vacate / renewed JML / amend findings: 30 days from Entry of judgment (Ala. R. Civ. P. 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e)). Cannot be extended (Rule 6(b)). District court 14 days; eviction and unlawful detainer 7 calendar days.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Motion to set aside default judgment
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Motion to set aside default judgment: 30 days from Entry of default judgment (Ala. R. Civ. P. 55(c)). Tolls under App. Rule 4(a)(3); 59.1 applies.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Appeal of interlocutory injunction, receivership, public-office, bond-validation, or juvenile order
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Appeal of interlocutory injunction, receivership, public-office, bond-validation, or juvenile order: 14 days from Entry of the order (Ala. R. App. P. 4(a)(1)(A)–(E)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Cross-appeal
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Cross-appeal: 14 days from Filing of first notice of appeal (or original 42 days, whichever later) (Ala. R. App. P. 4(a)(2)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Appeal of order granting or denying motion to compel arbitration
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Appeal of order granting or denying motion to compel arbitration: 42 days from Entry of the order (Ala. R. App. P. 4(d)). Appeal as of right.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Trial-court extension of appeal time for failure to learn of entry
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Trial-court extension of appeal time for failure to learn of entry: 30 days from Expiration of original appeal time (Ala. R. Civ. P. 77(d)). Excusable neglect based on lack of notice only.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Appeal of denial of campaign-contribution recusal motion
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Appeal of denial of campaign-contribution recusal motion: 30 days from Order denying recusal (Ala. Code § 12-24-3(d)). Civil actions; trial stayed if statutory threshold met.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Designation of clerk’s record; transcript purchase order and payment
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Designation of clerk’s record; transcript purchase order and payment: 7 days from Filing of notice of appeal (Ala. R. App. P. 10(b)(1), (2)). Appellee counter-designation 7 days after receipt.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Docket fee received by appellate clerk (e-filed notice)
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Docket fee received by appellate clerk (e-filed notice): 7 days from E-filing of notice of appeal (Ala. R. App. P. 12(a), 35A). $200 civil.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Clerk’s record completed
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Clerk’s record completed: 28 days from Filing of notice of appeal (Ala. R. App. P. 11(a)(1)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Reporter’s transcript filed
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Reporter’s transcript filed: 56 days from Filing of notice of appeal (Ala. R. App. P. 11(a)(2), 11(c)). Trial-court extensions cannot go beyond 84 days from the notice.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Statement of the evidence served (no transcript)
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Statement of the evidence served (no transcript): 28 days from Filing of notice of appeal (Ala. R. App. P. 10(d)). Objections 14 days after service.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Appellant’s brief
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Appellant’s brief: 28 days from Date on certificate of completion of the record (Ala. R. App. P. 31(a)). One extension up to 7 days (Rule 31(d)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief: 21 days from Filing of appellant’s brief (Ala. R. App. P. 31(a)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Reply brief
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Reply brief: 14 days from Filing of appellee’s brief (Ala. R. App. P. 31(a)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Appellant/cross-appellee brief in cross-appeal
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Appellant/cross-appellee brief in cross-appeal: 21 days from Filing of appellee/cross-appellant’s brief (Ala. R. App. P. 31(a)). Cross-reply 14 days after.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Motion to exceed word limit
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Motion to exceed word limit: 7 days from Before the brief’s due date (Ala. R. App. P. 28(j)(3)). Filed at least 7 days before due date.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Response to motion
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Response to motion: 7 days from Service of motion (Ala. R. App. P. 27(a)). Reply 7 days after response.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Application for rehearing (with brief)
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Application for rehearing (with brief): 14 days from Release of decision (Ala. R. App. P. 40(c)). Brief on original submission required.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Petition for certiorari to Supreme Court from Court of Civil Appeals
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Petition for certiorari to Supreme Court from Court of Civil Appeals: 14 days from Court of Civil Appeals decision, or its ruling on rehearing (Ala. R. App. P. 39(c)). Cannot be extended in civil cases (Rule 2(b)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Certificate of judgment issues
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Certificate of judgment issues: 18 days from Entry of appellate judgment (or denial of rehearing in courts of appeals) (Ala. R. App. P. 41(a)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Trial judge’s Rule 5 certification (presumptive)
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Trial judge’s Rule 5 certification (presumptive): 28 days from Entry of interlocutory order (Ala. R. App. P. 5(a)(1)). Later certification requires good-cause statement.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Petition for permission to appeal (Rule 5)
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Petition for permission to appeal (Rule 5): 14 days from Entry of trial judge’s certification (Ala. R. App. P. 5(a)(2)). Supreme Court cases only; answer 14 days.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Mandamus petition (presumptively reasonable time)
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Mandamus petition (presumptively reasonable time): 42 days from Entry of challenged order (Ala. R. App. P. 21(a)(3)). Later petitions must show good cause.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Supreme Court review of court of appeals ruling on original writ petition
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Supreme Court review of court of appeals ruling on original writ petition: 14 days from Grant or denial by court of appeals (Ala. R. App. P. 21(e)(2)).

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Automatic stay of execution
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Automatic stay of execution: 30 days from Entry of judgment (Ala. R. Civ. P. 62(a)). Not for injunction or receivership judgments; district court 14 days.

docs.t: Alabama appeal deadline — Jury demand by appellee in de novo appeal to circuit court
docs.x: Alabama appellate deadline. Jury demand by appellee in de novo appeal to circuit court: 14 days from Service of notice of appeal (Ala. Code § 12-12-71). Appellant must demand in the notice of appeal.

docs.t: Arkansas — 120 days to serve, and extensions must be sought in time
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. 120 days to serve, and extensions must be sought in time: Unserved defendants are dismissed at 120 days. An extension motion must be filed within the 120 days (or the current extension), and the order must be entered within 30 days after the motion or by the end of the period, whichever is later. Default judgments based on certified mail need a return receipt signed by the addressee or agent; unclaimed mail is not refusal. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 4(g)(1)(A)(ii), 4(i))

docs.t: Arkansas — Plead facts and attach the contract
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Plead facts and attach the contract: A complaint must state facts showing jurisdiction, venue, and entitlement to relief. Any written instrument a claim or defense is based on must be attached unless good cause is shown. An unspecified damages demand caps recovery below the federal diversity amount unless the demand shows more is sought. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 8(a), 10(d))

docs.t: Arkansas — 10-day motion responses, and hearings are waived
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. 10-day motion responses, and hearings are waived: Responses to motions are due 10 days after service and replies 5 days after the response. Each must include a brief supporting statement with citations or it can be struck. Unless counsel requests a hearing, the court can rule on the papers once the reply time runs. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 6(c), 7(b)(2), 78(c))

docs.t: Arkansas — Jury demand by 20 days before trial
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Jury demand by 20 days before trial: There is no automatic jury. File a written demand no later than 20 days before the trial date or the jury is waived. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 38(a), (c))

docs.t: Arkansas — Summary judgment cutoffs
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Summary judgment cutoffs: Summary-judgment motions must be filed at least 45 days before a scheduled trial absent leave. Responses are due 21 days after service, replies 14 days after the response, and no supplemental materials may follow the reply. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 56(a)–(c))

docs.t: Arkansas — Document subpoenas: 3 business days’ notice to the other side first
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Document subpoenas: 3 business days’ notice to the other side first: A subpoena for documents only must be served on all other parties at least 3 business days before it is served on the recipient, and everything produced must be shared promptly. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 45(b)(1))

docs.t: Arkansas — Voluntary nonsuit: easy once, fatal twice
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Voluntary nonsuit: easy once, fatal twice: A plaintiff may dismiss without prejudice as of right up to final submission, but only by court order. A second voluntary dismissal of the same claim is an adjudication on the merits unless all parties stipulate otherwise. Twelve months with no action of record invites dismissal for want of prosecution. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 41(a)–(b))

docs.t: Arkansas — Post-trial motions die on day 30, and the appeal clock starts
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Post-trial motions die on day 30, and the appeal clock starts: New-trial, JNOV, and amend-findings motions are due within 10 days after entry. If the judge has not ruled within 30 days after filing, the motion is deemed denied and the 30-day appeal period runs from that day, even if a hearing is scheduled later. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 50(b)(2), 52(b)(1), 59(b); Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 4(b)(1))

docs.t: Arkansas — Partial judgments need a Rule 54(b) certificate with findings
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Partial judgments need a Rule 54(b) certificate with findings: Without an executed Rule 54(b) certificate stating specific factual findings, an order leaving any claim or party unresolved is not appealable. Request the certificate within 14 days of entry. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 54(b); Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 2(a)(11))

docs.t: Arkansas — Notice of appeal must abandon unresolved claims
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Notice of appeal must abandon unresolved claims: A notice of appeal from a final order must state that the appellant abandons any pending but unresolved claim. That statement works as a dismissal with prejudice. (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 3(e)(vi))

docs.t: Arkansas — Directed-verdict motion at the close of all evidence
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Directed-verdict motion at the close of all evidence: In a jury case, a party without the burden of proof waives any sufficiency-of-the-evidence argument on appeal unless it moved for a directed verdict at the close of all the evidence, not just the opponent’s case. (Ark. R. Civ. P. 50(e))

docs.t: Arkansas — Pro hac vice: three cases a year and reciprocity
docs.x: Arkansas land mine. Pro hac vice: three cases a year and reciprocity: Arkansas courts must deny pro hac vice to a lawyer who appeared in 3 Arkansas cases in the prior 12 months. Lawyers from jurisdictions that do not admit Arkansas lawyers pro hac vice are not eligible. Each motion needs $200 paid in advance and a signed sponsor affidavit. (Ark. Bar Adm. R. XIV(a)–(c), (f))

docs.t: Arkansas anti-SLAPP — Citizen Participation in Government Act
docs.x: Arkansas anti-SLAPP. Citizen Participation in Government Act: Arkansas’s anti-SLAPP law is the Citizen Participation in Government Act, enacted by Act 1843 of 2005 as a new Subchapter 5 of Title 16, Chapter 63. It protects “privileged communications” and acts in furtherance of free speech or petitioning under the U.S. or Arkansas Constitution “in connection with an issue of public interest or concern.” Protected acts include statements made before or to a legislative, executive, or judicial proceeding, or about an issue under review by such a body. Privileged communications also include opinions and criticism of those proceedings and of public officers’ official acts. Statements made with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of falsity are excluded. The text comes from the enacted session law on the Legislature’s site, not the current codified Code, which is hosted on a commercial

docs.t: Arkansas anti-SLAPP — Immunity from civil liability
docs.x: Arkansas anti-SLAPP. Immunity from civil liability: A person making a privileged communication or a protected speech or petition act is immune from civil liability unless the statement was made knowing it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false. (Ark. Code Ann. § 16-63-504 (Act 1843 of 2005))

docs.t: Arkansas anti-SLAPP — The mechanism is a verification requirement, not a special motion
docs.x: Arkansas anti-SLAPP. The mechanism is a verification requirement, not a special motion: For any claim arising from a possible privileged communication or an act that could reasonably be seen as protected speech or petitioning, both the claimant and the claimant’s attorney must file, at the same time as the pleading, a written verification under oath. It must certify that they read the claim, that it is well grounded in fact and law after reasonable inquiry, that the act sued on is not a privileged communication, and that the claim is not brought for an improper purpose such as suppressing speech or petitioning, harassment, delay, or cost. (Ark. Code Ann. § 16-63-505 (Act 1843 of 2005))

docs.t: Arkansas anti-SLAPP — Strike for no verification; 10-day cure
docs.x: Arkansas anti-SLAPP. Strike for no verification; 10-day cure: An unverified claim must be stricken unless it is verified within 10 days after the omission is called to the attention of the claimant or the claimant’s attorney. If the claim is verified in violation of § 16-63-505, the court, on motion or on its own, must sanction the signers, the represented party, or both. Sanctions may include dismissal and reasonable expenses, including a reasonable attorney’s fee. (Ark. Code Ann. § 16-63-506(a), (b)(1) (Act 1843 of 2005))

docs.t: Arkansas anti-SLAPP — Discovery stay and 30-day hearing
docs.x: Arkansas anti-SLAPP. Discovery stay and 30-day hearing: Filing a motion to dismiss or strike under § 16-63-506 stays all discovery and pending hearings and motions. The hearing must be held within 30 days after service unless emergency matters require a later date. On motion and for good cause, the court may allow specified discovery or other proceedings to go forward. The Act sets no filing deadline for the motion. (Ark. Code Ann. § 16-63-507 (Act 1843 of 2005))

docs.t: Arkansas anti-SLAPP — Fees and damages
docs.x: Arkansas anti-SLAPP. Fees and damages: Fees come through the § 16-63-506(b)(1) sanction (reasonable expenses including attorney’s fees) for a falsely verified claim. Other compensatory damages require proof that the claim was brought or continued to harass, intimidate, punish, or maliciously inhibit protected speech or petitioning. The Act preserves any other recovery available by common law, statute, or rule. (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 16-63-506(b), -508 (Act 1843 of 2005))

docs.t: Arkansas anti-SLAPP — Appeal: no listed interlocutory appeal
docs.x: Arkansas anti-SLAPP. Appeal: no listed interlocutory appeal: The Act provides no immediate appeal, and Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 2(a) does not list orders under the Act among the appealable interlocutory orders. Its immunity exception, 2(a)(10), covers only sovereign immunity and the immunity of government officials. Whether Arkansas appellate courts have allowed an interlocutory appeal of an anti-SLAPP ruling by case law was not checked. (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 2(a); Ark. Code Ann. §§ 16-63-501 to -508)

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Notice of appeal
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Notice of appeal: 30 days from Entry (clerk’s file-stamp) of the judgment or order, or entry of the Rule 54(b) certificate (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 4(a)(1), 4(d); Admin. Order No. 2(b)(2)). File with the circuit clerk. Must include the abandonment statement for final orders.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Notice of cross-appeal
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Notice of cross-appeal: 10 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (or 30 days from entry of the order, whichever is later) (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 4(a)(2)). Use the later of the two dates.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Post-trial motions (JNOV, amend findings, new trial, alter or amend)
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Post-trial motions (JNOV, amend findings, new trial, alter or amend): 10 days from Entry of judgment (Ark. R. Civ. P. 50(b), 52(b), 59(b); Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 4(b)(1)). Deemed denied if not ruled on within 30 days after filing.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Notice of appeal after a post-trial motion
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Notice of appeal after a post-trial motion: 30 days from Entry of the order deciding the last motion, or the deemed-denial date (30th day after filing) (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 4(b)(1)). The deemed-denial date runs automatically.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Amend notice to appeal the post-trial ruling
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Amend notice to appeal the post-trial ruling: 30 days from Disposition or deemed denial of the motion (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 4(b)(2)). No additional fee.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Motion to extend appeal time for non-receipt of notice of judgment
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Motion to extend appeal time for non-receipt of notice of judgment: 180 days from Entry of the judgment (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 4(b)(3)). Relief is 14 days from entry of the extension order.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Rule 54(b) certificate motion
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Rule 54(b) certificate motion: 14 days from Entry of the partial judgment (Ark. R. Civ. P. 54(b)(2)). Deemed denied at 30 days; no certificate later than 45 days after judgment or 30 days after the motion, whichever is later.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Petition for permission to appeal privilege discovery order
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Petition for permission to appeal privilege discovery order: 14 days from Entry of the order (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 2(f)(1)). Calendar days; 10-page limit; response in 10 calendar days.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Appellee’s designation of additional record
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Appellee’s designation of additional record: 10 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 6(b)).

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Lodge the record
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Lodge the record: 90 days from Filing of the first notice of appeal (Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 5(a)). 30 days for injunction and receivership appeals; circuit court extensions capped at 7 months from the first notice.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Appellant’s brief
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Appellant’s brief: 40 days from Lodging of the record (Ark. Sup. Ct. R. 4-4(b)). One 7-day clerk extension available.

docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Response to a motion or petition: 10 days from Filing of the motion or petition (Ark. Sup. Ct. R. 2-1(d)). Calendar days.

docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Motion to reconsider an order on a motion: 18 days from Date of the order (Ark. Sup. Ct. R. 2-1(g)). Calendar days.

docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Petition for review in the Supreme Court: 10 days from End of the Court of Appeals rehearing period (Ark. Sup. Ct. R. 2-4(a)). Calendar days; 3-page limit. An early petition is held as tendered.

docs.t: Arkansas appeal deadline — Response to petition for review
docs.x: Arkansas appellate deadline. Response to petition for review: 10 days from Filing (or deemed filing) of the petition (Ark. Sup. Ct. R. 2-4(e)). Calendar days.

docs.t: Colorado — Notice of appeal is filed in the appellate court, 49 days after entry
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Notice of appeal is filed in the appellate court, 49 days after entry: Unlike federal practice, the notice goes to the clerk of the appellate court, with an advisory copy served on the trial court within the same time. Civil deadline: 49 days after entry of the judgment or order. If notice of entry was mailed or e-served, the time runs from that date. (C.A.R. 3(a), 4(a)(1), (5))

docs.t: Colorado — Post-trial motions: 14 days, and silence denies them at 63 days
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Post-trial motions: 14 days, and silence denies them at 63 days: A C.R.C.P. 59 motion is due 14 days after entry of judgment. Any extension must be requested within those 14 days. If the court does not rule within 63 days of the last motion, the motion is deemed denied and the 49-day appeal clock starts that day without any order. (C.R.C.P. 59(a), (j); C.A.R. 4(a)(3))

docs.t: Colorado — A suit can start by service, but the complaint must follow within 14 days
docs.x: Colorado land mine. A suit can start by service, but the complaint must follow within 14 days: An action may be commenced by serving a summons and complaint before filing. The complaint must then be filed within 14 days, or the service is void without notice and fees may be taxed against the plaintiff or counsel. The defendant waives the requirement by responding without reserving it. (C.R.C.P. 3(a))

docs.t: Colorado — No punitive-damages claim in the complaint
docs.x: Colorado land mine. No punitive-damages claim in the complaint: An exemplary-damages claim may not be included in any initial claim for relief. It can be added by amendment only after Rule 26 initial disclosures are exchanged and the plaintiff shows prima facie proof of a triable issue. Exemplary damages are capped at the amount of actual damages awarded, subject to the statute’s exceptions. (C.R.S. § 13-21-102(1)(a), (1.5)(a))

docs.t: Colorado — Losing a tort case on a Rule 12(b) motion shifts the defense fees
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Losing a tort case on a Rule 12(b) motion shifts the defense fees: When a tort action for death or injury to person or property is dismissed before trial on a defendant’s C.R.C.P. 12(b) motion, the defendant gets a judgment for reasonable attorney fees. This does not apply if the motion is converted to summary judgment, or to a good-faith claim pleaded as seeking to change or establish the law and identifying the precedent at issue. (C.R.S. § 13-17-201(1)–(2))

docs.t: Colorado — Professional-negligence claims need a certificate of review in 60 days
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Professional-negligence claims need a certificate of review in 60 days: In a damages action based on a licensed professional’s alleged negligence, the plaintiff’s lawyer must file a certificate of review for each professional named, and for any firm that employed one, within 60 days after service. The certificate declares that an expert was consulted and concluded the claim does not lack substantial justification. (C.R.S. § 13-20-602(1), (3))

docs.t: Colorado — Rule 16 runs on the “at issue” date, not a scheduling conference
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Rule 16 runs on the “at issue” date, not a scheduling conference: No later than 14 days after the case is at issue, lead counsel must confer. Rule 26(a)(1) disclosures are due 28 days after the at-issue date. A proposed Case Management Order, in editable format, is due 42 days after the at-issue date and at least 7 days before the case management conference. Formal discovery generally cannot begin until the Case Management Order is served. Plaintiff’s counsel is the “responsible attorney” for these filings. (C.R.C.P. 16(b)(1)–(3), (d); 26(a)(1), (d))

docs.t: Colorado — Tight presumptive discovery limits
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Tight presumptive discovery limits: Without a court order for good cause and proportionality, each party gets one deposition of each adverse party plus two other persons (experts excluded), 30 single-question interrogatories, 20 document requests, and 20 requests for admission (plus up to 50 genuineness-of-document requests) per adverse party. Non-expert depositions are limited to 6 hours, and retained-expert depositions also to 6 hours. (C.R.C.P. 26(b)(2), (b)(4)(A); 30(d)(2))

docs.t: Colorado — Expert disclosures count back from trial, and testimony is limited to the report
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Expert disclosures count back from trial, and testimony is limited to the report: Unless the Case Management Order says otherwise, the claiming party’s expert disclosures are due 126 days before trial. The defending party’s are due 28 days later, but no earlier than 98 days before trial if the claimant disclosed early. Rebuttal is due 77 days before trial. A retained expert’s signed report must include all opinions, sources, the fee agreement, and an itemization of fees (supplemented 14 days before trial). Direct testimony is limited to what the report discloses in detail. (C.R.C.P. 26(a)(2)(B)(I), (C))

docs.t: Colorado — Pretrial-motion cutoffs: 91 days for summary judgment, 70 for C.R.E. 702
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Pretrial-motion cutoffs: 91 days for summary judgment, 70 for C.R.E. 702: Summary-judgment motions and motions to determine a question of law are due no later than 91 days before trial. C.R.E. 702 challenges to experts are due 70 days before trial, and other pretrial motions, including motions in limine, 35 days before trial, unless the court orders otherwise. (C.R.C.P. 16(c); 56(h) (Rule Change 2025(12), eff. Jan. 1, 2026))

docs.t: Colorado — Every motion must certify conferral, and briefs are page-limited
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Every motion must certify conferral, and briefs are page-limited: Before filing almost any motion, counsel must confer with opposing counsel and self-represented parties, and the motion must open with a conferral certification. Legal authority goes in the motion itself, not a separate brief. Limits: 15 pages for motions and responses and 10 for replies; 25 and 15 pages for Rule 12(b)(1)–(2) and Rule 56 motions. Responses are due in 21 days (14 if filed within 42 days of trial). Replies are due in 7 days (14 for summary judgment). An unopposed motion must say so in its title. Except for Rule 12 and Rule 56 motions, failure to file a response may be treated as a confession of the motion. (C.R.C.P. 121 § 1-15(1), (3), (8), (9) (Rule Change 2024(03)))

docs.t: Colorado — Untimely or missing disclosure means exclusion
docs.x: Colorado land mine. Untimely or missing disclosure means exclusion: A party that fails without substantial justification to make a Rule 26(a) or 26(e) disclosure cannot use the undisclosed evidence at trial or on a Rule 56 motion. The 2015 amendment frames the exception as a failure that has not caused and will not cause significant harm, or preclusion that would be disproportionate to that harm, in place of the older “harmless” wording. The collected text is a redline only, so confirm the current wording. The court may add other proportionate sanctions and fees. (C.R.C.P. 37(c)(1))

docs.t: Colorado anti-SLAPP — Statute: C.R.S. § 13-20-1101 (special motion to dismiss), effective July 1, 2019
docs.x: Colorado anti-SLAPP. Statute: C.R.S. § 13-20-1101 (special motion to dismiss), effective July 1, 2019: Colorado’s anti-SLAPP law is C.R.S. § 13-20-1101, added by H.B. 19-1324 effective July 1, 2019. It protects any “act in furtherance of a person’s right of petition or free speech … in connection with a public issue.” That includes statements made before, or about an issue under review by, a legislative, executive, judicial, or other official proceeding; statements in a public place or public forum on an issue of public interest; and any other conduct furthering petition or speech rights on a public issue. “Complaint,” “defendant,” and “plaintiff” include cross-complaints, cross-defendants, petitions, and respondents. (C.R.S. § 13-20-1101(1)–(2); L. 2019, H.B. 19-1324)

docs.t: Colorado anti-SLAPP — Standard: the plaintiff must show a reasonable likelihood of prevailing
docs.x: Colorado anti-SLAPP. Standard: the plaintiff must show a reasonable likelihood of prevailing: A covered claim is dismissed on a special motion unless the plaintiff establishes a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on the claim. The court considers the pleadings and the supporting and opposing affidavits. If the plaintiff meets the standard, neither the ruling nor the fact that it was made is admissible later in the case or in any later proceeding, and it does not change any burden of proof. (C.R.S. § 13-20-1101(3))

docs.t: Colorado anti-SLAPP — Deadline 63 days after service; hearing within 28 days; discovery stayed
docs.x: Colorado anti-SLAPP. Deadline 63 days after service; hearing within 28 days; discovery stayed: File the special motion within 63 days after service of the complaint, or later if the court allows it on terms. The hearing must be set no more than 28 days after service of the motion unless the court’s docket requires a later date. All discovery is stayed when notice of the motion is filed and remains stayed until notice of entry of the order ruling on it. On noticed motion and good cause, the court may allow specified discovery. The official C.R.S. annotations note that the special motion is also available in county court (VOA Sunset Hous. LP v. D’Angelo, 2024 COA 61). (C.R.S. § 13-20-1101(5), (6); annotation to § 13-20-1101)

docs.t: Colorado anti-SLAPP — Fees: mandatory for a winning defendant; for a plaintiff only if the motion was frivolous
docs.x: Colorado anti-SLAPP. Fees: mandatory for a winning defendant; for a plaintiff only if the motion was frivolous: A defendant who wins the special motion is entitled to attorney fees and costs. A plaintiff who defeats the motion gets costs and reasonable fees only if the court finds the motion frivolous or solely intended to cause unnecessary delay, under C.R.S. title 13, article 17, part 1. A winning defendant does not get fees under this section if the claim was brought under the Open Meetings Law (part 4 of article 6 of title 24) or the Colorado Open Records Act, though fees under §§ 24-6-402(9)(b) and 24-72-204 remain available. (C.R.S. § 13-20-1101(4))

docs.t: Colorado anti-SLAPP — Exemptions: government enforcement, public-interest suits, and commercial speech
docs.x: Colorado anti-SLAPP. Exemptions: government enforcement, public-interest suits, and commercial speech: The statute does not apply to (1) enforcement actions by the state or a subdivision, or actions to protect against an imminent threat to health or safety; (2) actions brought solely in the public interest that meet three listed conditions; or (3) claims against a seller or lessor of goods or services based on factual statements about its own or a competitor’s business made to sell, or made to actual or potential buyers (with a carve-out involving telephone corporations before the PUC). The public-interest and commercial-speech exemptions do not apply to news media, book or journal publishers, or claims based on dramatic, literary, musical, political, or artistic works. (C.R.S. § 13-20-1101(8))

docs.t: Colorado anti-SLAPP — Appeal goes to the Court of Appeals, but read Hinds v. Foreman (2026)
docs.x: Colorado anti-SLAPP. Appeal goes to the Court of Appeals, but read Hinds v. Foreman (2026): An order granting or denying the special motion is appealable to the Court of Appeals under C.R.S. § 13-4-102.2, except when the trial court denies the motion because the case is exempt under subsection (8). The 2026 C.R.S. editor’s note reports that Hinds v. Foreman, 2026 CO 9, held § 13-20-1101(7) and § 13-4-102.2 unconstitutional to the extent they let the Court of Appeals review final judgments, because that conflicts with Colo. Const. art. VI, § 17 and C.R.S. § 13-6-310(1) (county-court appeals go to district court). Read Hinds before taking an anti-SLAPP appeal from county court. The statute sets no appeal deadline of its own. Assume C.A.R. 4(a)’s 49 days and confirm. The annotations report that a timely motion to reconsider a denial tolls the appeal time (Said v. Magdy, 2024 COA 109). (C.R.

docs.x: District of Columbia land mine. docs.x: District of Columbia land mine. D.D.C. admission does not get you into Superior Court: Only members of the D.C. Court of Appeals bar may practice in the D.C. courts. docs.x: District of Columbia land mine. Small-claims judgments: no appeal of right: Review of a Small Claims and Conciliation Branch judgment is by application for allowance of an appeal, not by notice of appeal. (D.C. Code § 11-721(c))
